idiom_name: small interface + struct over nats.go Conn.Request or amqp091-go
implementation_notes: Go has no proxy generation, so the gateway is a plain interface (InventoryGateway with CheckStock(ctx, sku)) implemented by a struct that owns the client. On NATS the request-reply mechanics are already solved: nc.Request(subject, payload, timeout) creates a private inbox, attaches the reply subject, returns the first reply and distinguishes nats.ErrNoResponders from nats.ErrTimeout, so the gateway method becomes a thin typed wrapper that maps those errors into domain errors. On AMQP you write the mechanics yourself - declare an exclusive reply queue, publish with ReplyTo and CorrelationId, loop until the correlation id matches (the Go RPC tutorial's fibonacciRPC is exactly that hand-written gateway). Nothing in either route gives you the domain interface: that part is always yours.
pitfalls: nats.ErrTimeout and nats.ErrNoResponders are ordinary errors, and a timeout says only that the answer did not arrive in time - the gateway must map both into domain errors instead of letting callers compare against broker sentinels.
Core NATS replies are at-most-once: a reply that is lost is gone, so a timed-out call must be treated as an unknown outcome and the remote operation made idempotent before any retry.

The AMQP client opens a connection, a channel and an exclusive reply queue per request in the tutorial - a real gateway must pool connections and serialize use of a single channel rather than repeating that per call.
Swallowing ctx.Err() from a cancelled request hides the fact that the broker-side work may still be running.
